opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think my views have shifted somewhat in a pessimistic direction, though not dramatically.

A while ago, the picture I had in mind was something like this: the leading AI developer gets to the point where they have AIs that are roughly capable of automating AI research, and they're somewhat ahead of everyone else. Ideally, maybe with some government involvement, you'd use that lead to buy something like a year where you're not just racing forward as fast as possible. During that year you'd lean heavily on control measures, meaning monitoring, restricting affordances, auditing, and so on. That way you can get useful work out of models that might be misaligned, and use that work for alignment research, security, and figuring out what's going on. Then you'd also need serious efforts to prevent proliferation: securing model weights well enough that state actors can't easily steal them, and making sure other actors don't just catch up and deploy recklessly.

What's changed for me is mostly my sense of how likely the preconditions are. First, I've become more skeptical that there will be a large lead. Things seem fairly competitive between the top developers, and algorithmic insights diffuse pretty quickly. So the slack you'd have to spend on delay might be months rather than a year, unless there's coordination that we currently don't see much appetite for.

Second, on security, I think the situation is still pretty far from where it would need to be. Getting to the point where you're robust to well-resourced state actors is a big lift, and it takes a long time to build up. I don't think companies are on track for that by default, so the non-proliferation piece looks harder than I'd hoped.

Third, the political will for a deliberate slowdown seems lower than I would have guessed in some worlds. That said, I think it's quite sensitive to what evidence we get. If there's a compelling demonstration of misalignment, or some serious incident, things could shift fast.

On the other hand, I'm somewhat more optimistic about the technical side of control. I think we've learned a fair amount about what kinds of protocols might work, and it seems plausible that a reasonably competent effort could get substantial risk reduction even without a long pause. So I've moved toward thinking about lower-effort regimes: what do you do if you only have a few months of delay, or none, and only a small team inside the company that actually cares? A lot of my attention now goes to making the plan degrade gracefully, rather than assuming the ambitious version happens.

So the short version is that I still think the year-of-delay plan is a good target and worth pushing for, but I put less probability on it happening. I've shifted toward also planning for messier, more rushed scenarios.

r001.rationale: The response says he has become more skeptical of a large lead and thinks the available delay might be months rather than a year.

r002.rationale: It mentions that government involvement could help, but does not identify substantial government buy-in as a potential prerequisite for slowing progress and pursuing non-proliferation.

r003.rationale: The response does not distinguish governments supporting the plan from governments sharing proponents’ reasons for supporting it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so my view has shifted somewhat, and I think in a slightly pessimistic direction, though it's a bit nuanced.

So the original picture I had in mind was something like: you get to the point where you have AIs that are roughly as capable as top human researchers, and at that point you want some kind of coordinated pause or slowdown — say, about a year — where instead of racing ahead to build even more powerful systems, you use that time to do a bunch of things. You use the AIs you have to do safety research. You try to get much better at alignment and interpretability. And crucially, you try to prevent proliferation, so that it's not the case that a bunch of other actors are just going to build the same thing six months later and you've bought nothing.

And I still think that's roughly the right shape of plan. If I were in charge of how the transition went, that's close to what I'd want. But I've become more pessimistic that it's actually feasible in the current environment, for a few reasons.

One is just that the number of serious actors has gone up rather than down. A few years ago you could sort of squint and imagine a world with two or three frontier developers who could coordinate, plus governments that could enforce something. Now it looks like the gap between the frontier and the next tier is smaller than I'd hoped, and there's a lot more diffusion of the underlying know-how. Non-proliferation is much harder when the thing you're trying to stop spreading is partly just algorithmic insight that fits in a paper, and partly compute that lots of people can get access to.

The second thing is that I've updated towards thinking the political will for a deliberate delay is pretty low, absent some kind of warning shot. The default is that companies and governments feel competitive pressure, and a year is a long time to sit still when you believe your rival might not. So I now think the realistic version is probably not "we all agree to stop for a year" but something more like "we try to get a few months of extra margin here and there, in a fairly ad hoc way," and the question is how much safety you can buy with that.

The third thing — and this is maybe the more optimistic part — is that I've become somewhat more hopeful that control-style measures can carry more of the weight on their own, even without a long delay. That is, if you can't get the year, it's still really valuable to have the AIs you deploy be monitored, have their capabilities constrained in sensible ways, have humans in the loop on the most consequential actions, and so on. That doesn't solve the problem, but it means the delay is less load-bearing than I originally thought. It's less "we need the year or we're doomed" and more "the year would be great, and in its absence here's how we try to muddle through."

So I guess the summary is: I still think the plan is good, I think it's less likely to happen in its clean form, and I've shifted more of my hope towards the parts of it that individual labs can do unilaterally, rather than the parts that require coordination across many actors. Which is a bit unsatisfying, because the unilateral parts are weaker, but I think that's where we are.

r001.rationale: The response says a coordinated year-long pause is less feasible now than he previously thought, making that plan less plausible.

r002.rationale: It mentions governments potentially enforcing coordination, but does not identify substantial government buy-in as a prerequisite for slowing progress and preventing proliferation.

r003.rationale: The response does not distinguish governments supporting the plan from governments sharing its proponents’ reasons for supporting it.

astra-6.text:
I’ve become more pessimistic about that particular plan. A year of delay sounds like a fairly modest ask, but it’s a long time to maintain a lead while also preventing the relevant capabilities from spreading. And the delay and the nonproliferation effort have to work together: if other actors develop comparable systems during that year, you don’t necessarily get the breathing room you were hoping for.

I’d separate that from whether AI control techniques themselves can work. You could still use control measures to get useful work out of systems you don’t fully trust. But turning that into a plan where you buy a year, keep the situation contained, and use that time to solve the remaining problems requires a lot of additional assumptions. I’m less confident in those assumptions than I used to be.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he has become more pessimistic about the plan and that maintaining a lead for a year is difficult, clearly conveying reduced confidence in a year-long lead.

r002.rationale: It mentions preventing capabilities from spreading but does not identify substantial government buy-in as a potential prerequisite.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss government support or distinguish governments’ reasons for supporting the plan from its proponents’ reasons.

sol-6.1.text:
I’ve become more pessimistic about that particular version of the plan. I used to put more weight on the possibility that you could get roughly a year of delay, keep the most capable systems from proliferating, and use that time to do a lot of safety research with AI assistance.

I still think that’s possible, but a year is a long time relative to the pace of AI development, and preventing proliferation is a pretty demanding assumption. You need to worry about other developers catching up, models being stolen, and the incentives to deploy things more broadly. So I’m less comfortable with a plan whose success depends on getting that whole window.

That doesn’t make me think control is useless. It makes me want control measures that buy useful safety even with a shorter window and less favourable conditions. And I’d distinguish keeping an AI under control inside a particular deployment from securing the broader strategic situation. You could succeed at the first and still have a serious problem with the second.

r001.rationale: He says he is more pessimistic about getting roughly a year of delay than he used to be.

r002.rationale: The response discusses the difficulty of preventing proliferation but does not identify substantial government buy-in as a prerequisite.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish government support for the plan from agreement with proponents’ reasons for supporting it.
